stories.title: 25 years North Macedonian peace: reconciliation in sight?
stories.summary: A quarter of a century after the Ohrid Framework Agreement ended North Macedonia's 2001 conflict, analysts warn that peace between ethnic communities remains fragile.
stories.post: 📰 NEWS: 25 years North Macedonian peace: reconciliation in sight? A quarter of a century after the Ohrid Framework Agreement ended North Macedonia's 2001 conflict, analysts warn that peace between ethnic communities remains fragile. Source: DW World.
article_sentences: The guns fell silent in 2001, but North Macedonia is still grappling with the legacy of its ethnic conflict.
Twenty-five years after the Ohrid Framework Agreement ended the fighting, ethnic Macedonians and Albanians live in peace, yet analysts say genuine reconciliation remains unattained.
The six-month conflict that erupted in February 2001 is often described as the final chapter of former Yugoslavia's violent breakup.

But unlike the wars in Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Kosovo, it was contained before it could spiral into a larger tragedy, thanks in large part to a political compromise brokered by NATO, the United States and leading EU countries.
Тwenty-five years later, the political order that emerged from the Ohrid Framework Agreement is entering a new phase.
When the conservative Macedonian VMRO-DPMNE party returned to power two years ago, the Democratic Union for Integration (DUI), the main ethnic Albanian party, went into opposition.

This development ended two decades of governing influence for Ali Ahmeti, who transformed himself from leader of the ethnic Albanian National Liberation Army (NLA) during the 2001 conflict into one of the country's most influential political figures.
Ahmeti, who swapped his guerrilla uniform for tailored black suits and white shirts after the Ohrid Agreement, now argues that ethnic relations have deteriorated over the past two years.

"Attacks on the official use of the Albanian language, the abolition of equitable and adequate representation, the weakening of mechanisms designed to prevent majoritarian rule and the promotion of a monoethnic concept of the state are serious signals about the direction in which the country is moving," he said in a statement marking August 2, North Macedonia's national holiday.
Home to a large ethnic Albanian minority, North Macedonia has spent much of the past quarter-century trying to balance its ethnic diversity within a stable political system.
According to the latest census, Albanians make up over a quarter of North Macedonia's population of 1.8 million.
For Bujar Osmani, a senior DUI official and former foreign minister, the key question is no longer how much of the Ohrid Agreement has been implemented, but whether its gains can be preserved.
